ASK-TELL-ASK when sharing information

. Tell the most important message first
. Begin with a simple, general statement of how sick s/he is (think: what two things do they really need to know?)
. Do not use jargon
. Be honest and direct
. Use short phrases
. Use diagrams if appropriate
. Pause frequently—Allow time to process information.
. Give prognosis, if known, or share frustration about uncertainty. Try to identify what (and when) will indicate improvement or worsening.

• Be sure to check family understanding and/or reaction after sharing news • Validate the complexity or difficulty of the news (e.g., “I have shared a lot of information with you--let me stop now and see what questions you might have”)
ASK--Always ask a question before sharing information. Listen to response without interrupting, and reflect back.
TELL—Be brief and clear when sharing information ASK--Check in with a follow-up question
· Observe reactions and respond to emotion.
· Remember there are often emotions in questions and statement—respond to emotion first.
· Answer honestly if family asks “is s/he going to die?”
· Avoid terms like “exacerbate,” “pressors,” and “extubate”
· Use drawings or diagrams when helpful
· Ask permission to move on in the conversation or to make suggestions
· Notice emotion, pause and listen
· Use nonverbal responses to emotion: pause, offer tissues, comforting gestures, such as a touch on the shoulder or arm, if appropriate
· Use verbal responses to emotion by validating emotion.
· Avoid premature reassurances. Instead, explore their emotions and provide support.
· Support hope

· Allow patient/family to speak without interruption · Use open-ended questions and allow time to respond · Reflective listening: reflect what you observe or hear with a statement
· To explore their thoughts further, use “tell me more” · Invite questions
· Get to know your patient as an individual. What was life like before they became ill? What are their values, interests, and important relationships?

· Explore what the patient would consider a good quality of life
· Instead of listing treatment options, use open questions to understand goals
· Avoid “what do you want” and instead, ask “what would s/he think”
· Understand values and goals before discussing specific treatments
· When patients or family ask for specific treatments or express their goals, find out more by asking "tell me more about that" or ask "why do you feel she/ he would make that choice?”
· Explore and discuss likely outcome of treatments they are describing
